Title: Should You Wash Your Face with Salt Water?
Occasionally washing your face with salt water can exfoliate your skin and remove dead skin cells.
However, doing it too often may dry out your skin.
Ever returned from a beach vacation with your skin (and hair) looking bright and soft?
You might have wondered whether you could replicate that effect at home by washing your face and spritzing your hair with salt water from the sea.
Perhaps you’ve come across the TikTok videos suggesting that washing your face with sea salt water can get rid of acne and help you renew that fresh-off-the-beach look.
But should you try it?
Is all that salt safe for your hair and skin?

Before you swap your regular face wash for a splash of the sea, drop anchor and keep reading to find out what dermatologists have to say about using salt water on your face, including what it can and can’t do for your skin.
Salt water has been recognized for its ability to disinfect and cleanse skin since ancient Egypt, says Snehal Amin, MD, FAAD.

Amin, a board certified dermatologist and the co-founder and Surgical Director of MDCS Dermatology, explains that salt water is responsible for making skin feel smoother and drier after a day at the beach.
As for the benefits of salt water for skin?
“Salt acts as a mechanical exfoliant and scrub, removing dead skin cells.
This leaves the skin feeling smoother, softer, and brighter.
Through osmotic actions, salts absorb toxins and draw out dirt and oil.
Improved pore size is another benefit,” says Amin.

But before you load up on packages of salt, know that washing your face with salt water should be reserved for occasional use, according to Azadeh Shirazi, MD, a board certified dermatologist at La Jolla Dermatology and Laser Surgery Center.
Without a doubt, most people would probably love to have cleaner, softer, smoother skin, not to mention pores that appear smaller.
Both experts agree that salt water works best for people with oily or acne-prone skin, though it may not actually treat acne.
“I don’t consider it as a treatment for acne on its own,” Shirazi emphasizes.

While you might have encountered Internet guidance or TikTok videos promoting homemade salt water as an easy and miraculous solution for all your skin concerns, that’s not exactly the case.
Washing your face with salt water can be harsh and irritating, according to Shirazi, who warns that overuse can compromise your skin barrier.
“This can worsen some skin conditions like acne and eczema, or potentially cause hyperpigmentation and scarring.
It may also delay proper treatment and care from a dermatologist,” cautions Shirazi.
And again, salt can be harsh, so it could dry your skin and potentially lead to irritation and flaking.
Shirazi recommends using professionally formulated products if you’re prone to dry skin.
These are safer for your skin and may also work better than plain salt water.
Another important thing to consider before you try the saltwater trend is that it may not have the desired effect.
A homemade saltwater concoction doesn’t provide the same benefits as ocean water does, in other words.
Salt water from the actual ocean doesn’t just contain salt.
It also contains natural minerals like magnesium, calcium, and potassium.
These minerals, which are more than likely responsible for the skin benefits, are also hard to replicate at home, as Shirazi points out.

If you want to try washing your face with salt water, keep in mind that it’s best to avoid overdoing it, as this can lead to dry and damaged skin.
You might, for example, start by trying a saltwater wash once or twice a week to see how your skin handles it.
Amin also recommends skipping the scrubbing when using salt on your face.
“Salt is corrosive and can damage the skin when applied in high concentrations for an excessive period of time.
My basic advice is that a salt scrub is fine for the body but best to avoid for the face,” says Amin.

If you experience lingering dryness or irritation in the days after washing your face with salt water, it’s also best to get advice from a dermatologist.
A dermatologist can help identify and treat skin concerns, and they can also offer more guidance on recognizing your skin type and caring for your skin.
While a frolic in the ocean can leave your skin feeling amazing, replicating the magic of the sea at home and washing your face with DIY ocean water may not have the same effect.
All the same, salt water can still benefit your skin.
If you’re going to try it, go easy on the salt and use salt water sparingly to avoid drying out your skin.
A dermatologist can offer guidance if you want more support treating acne or other skin issues.
